"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural science (green chemistry, reverse logistics)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (materials synthesis and fertilizer release kinetics)",
"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) to synthesize new phosphate phases, primarily K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. The motivation is to provide novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and/or potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate, making it a soil conditioner, while addressing the problem of millions of tons of eggshells produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces, with the applied energy large enough to break the reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration to form a new structure. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, among other non-crystalline compounds and also CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, all these phosphates may exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations, influenced by the size of the metal cation and its charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. In addition, the solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process, ensuring huge savings during the production process. The materials and methods section describes the collection of eggshells from the authors' homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process, and the KH2PO4 supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter, using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, performed firstly for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h, in order to evaluate acid-basic reactions between these precursors. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulate commercial products, obtained in a steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in a 10 mL beaker immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring, with aliquots of 1.2 mL collected at different times (from 15 min to 30 days) to evaluate the release behavior and allow the calculation of a release kinetic model of Ca, K and P. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014), with each Petri dish of diameter 8.6 cm receiving 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil to achieve the desired density of 1.2 g.cm-3, and 15 mL deionized water added to achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity. The scanned images are converted to black-and-white binary images, using a threshold color value, and the area of the high P-zone is quantified using the histogram command. Soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in a plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil with 75% water saturation, performed at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days, using a single pellet for each container, with the pellet weight standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. After each release period the solid residues samples were removed from the soil and characterized by XRD; potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods, respectively; and phosphorus was extracted from soil using Mehlich 1 method. A colorimetric analysis of molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus released content into the solution, and potassium and calcium released content were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS), with a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T instrument, in flame atomization mode. The results show that the XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling, between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm, produce a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, with CaKPO4 more evident after 24 h of milling. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events, with the first step at 200°C associated to crystallization water loss and the second step at 300°C corresponding to polycondensation, concomitant with structural water loss, with the residual mass (89%) regarding to KPO3 formation consistent to the theoretical (87%). The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps, with a first mass loss step below 300 °C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation, and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700 °C. In the case of milled samples, three mass loss events are observed, with the first step centered at 280°C related to crystallization water loss, the second step centered at 420°C associated to partial structural water loss and structure dimerization, and the final step centered at 710°C corresponding to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. All samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700 °C, but in the samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed, suggesting that low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite to form calcium potassium phosphates. The 31P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate, with the shift at δ = 3.28 ppm and δ = 2.82 ppm reported to calcium phosphates compounds, and the signal at δ = 0.74 ppm related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with the KCaPO4 formation. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%), and phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples, showing that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. On the other hand, calcium release is rather different for eggshell to the milled samples, with the kinetic extremely slow in comparison, evidencing the solubility of phosphates formed. The nutrients release curves were fitted using the linear form of pseudo-first order, pseudo-second order and intraparticle diffusion models, with phosphorus and potassium presenting better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering 'R 2 ' and the values related to concentration at equilibrium time 'qe' and 'experimental qe'. For both nutrients there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing and certainly related to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was also evaluated in soil, with the temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicating a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor, while for sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days) corresponding to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample. An extra experiment was done to visualize the P diffusion zone and comparison with KH2PO4 and Struvite, with struvite not able to release any phosphorus at day 2, while sample 2h/600rpm the P diffusion reach a value of 1.99 cm a significant value compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4, with the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm being intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample. These results corroborate with citric acid solution release essays and attest efficient use of 2 h/600 rpm sample as a source of bioavailable calcium compared to the precursor eggshell, with the slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification, especially under pH 5. The conclusions indicate that based on the reverse logistic and green chemistry this study proposes the use of eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees a better nutrient management, playing on the solubility of calcium, potassium and phosphorus, with a mechanochemical process used, free of solvent, and presenting no unwanted subproduct, and new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4 presenting in citric acid solution a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The XRD patterns were obtained using an XRD 6000 diffractometer (Shimadzu), with the relative intensity of the diffraction peaks registered in the angular range (2θ) of 3-40°, using a Cu Kα incident beam (λ = 0.1546 nm) and scanning speed of 2° min-1 at 30 kV voltage and 40 mA current. The studies of the crystallization behavior were carried out using a TA Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) (TA Q100 Controller) with refrigerated cooling system (RCS), and the thermal degradation of samples was evaluated in the 25°C -600°C range using a Q500 analyzer (TA Instruments, New Castle, DE, USA) under synthetic air flow of 60 mL.min-1 (80% N2 and 20% O2) with a heating rate of 10°C.min-1. The thermogravimetric analyses were performed in a Thermogravimetric Analyzer TGA-Q500 (TA Instruments, USA) under synthetic air atmosphere (N2/O2) at a flow rate of 60/40 mL/min and using platinum crucibles, with the temperature range used being ~20 to 900 °C at 10 °C min-1. {
"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural science (reverse logistics, mechanochemistry, fertilizer science)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (materials synthesis, characterization, and release kinetics)",
"executive_summary": "This study proposes an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The synthesis is achieved through a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (a source of calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The resulting K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases provide better nutrient management of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) when applied to soil systems. When applied, the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important source of bioavailable P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The introduction establishes reverse logistics as an important instrument for applying shared responsibility for product lifecycles, citing Tibben and Lembke (2002), and highlights eggshells as important food industry wastes and excellent CaCO3 sources (Byeon, 2016). The solid-state mechanochemical activation applies mechanical energy to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces, with applied energy large enough to break reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, among other non-crystalline compounds and CO2 from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, these phosphates may exhibit different solubility according to bonds between metal cations, influenced by cation size and charge, affecting reticular energy (Jenkins et al., 1999). Experimental release studies reveal KH2PO4 exhibits much faster solubilization than calcium or calcium-potassium phosphates. Composed solely of fertilizer components (HPO4 2-/PO4 3-, Ca 2+, K+), the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, delaying bioavailability of P and K while improving Ca bioavailability. The solvent-free environment produces no liquid or solid waste, ensuring huge savings during production (Mujumdar and Huang, 2007). The materials and methods describe eggshells collected from authors' homes, washed with water, dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before grinding; KH2PO4 PA supplied from Vetec. The milling used a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7) with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. Essays were performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, first for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h at 600 rpm, then at 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming eggshells are mainly CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, 24 h at 250 °C), determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material was pelletized to simulate commercial products, obtained in a steel pelletizer applying 5 bar pressure, standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in a 10 mL beaker immersed in 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. Aliquots of 1.2 mL at different times (15 min to 30 days) were collected to evaluate release behavior and calculate a release kinetic model of Ca, K, and P. Phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes (8.6 cm diameter) containing 78 g of dry, sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil to achieve density of 1.2 g/cm³, with 15 mL deionized water added to achieve 70% of maximum soil water retention capacity. Papers were scanned and analyzed using GNU Image Manipulation Program v. 2.6.11. Soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in plastic containers with 50 g of sandy soil (75% water saturation) at 3, 7, 15, and 30 days, using a single pellet for each container, standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. After each release period, solid residues were characterized by XRD; K and Ca were extracted from soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods, respectively; P was extracted using Mehlich 1 method (Embrapa, 1979). Colorimetric analysis of molybdenum blue quantified P released content (Murphy and Riley, 1962), while K and Ca were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS) with a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T instrument. The results and discussion present XRD patterns (Fig. 1) showing milling between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% CaCO3) from 2 h and 400 rpm produces a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF database n° 22-1218) and possibly CaKPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002). Below these milling parameters, only reactant diffraction patterns are found, indicating no evidence of chemical reaction. There is a direct relationship between time and milling speed and increasing total energy. Only minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction, and as milling time increases, secondary reactions begin, such as mechanochemical dehydroxylation of newly formed phosphates. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: the first at 200°C associated with crystallization water loss, and the second at 300°C corresponding to polycondensation with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regarding KPO3 formation is consistent with theoretical (87%) (Fig. 2). Thermal degradation of eggshell has two steps: first below 300°C attributed to moisture elimination with organic membrane degradation, and second related to calcite decomposition below 700°C (Cree and Rutter, 2015; Omari et al., 2016). For milled samples (Fig. 2), three mass loss events are observed: first centered at 280°C related to crystallization water loss, second at 420°C associated with partial structural water loss and structure dimerization, and final at 710°C corresponding to final structural water loss and structure polycondensation (Vlase et al., 2005). All samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700°C, but in samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed, suggesting low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade total calcite. Figure 3 shows milled samples were calcined to characterize solid fractions after each main loss mechanism (280°C, 420°C, 710°C). In all cases, similar thermal behavior related to crystalline phase formation was identified, except for milling during 2 h at 600 rpm, which has an unclear phosphate phase but after thermal treatment at 280°C slightly changes matching with K3CaH(PO4)2 phase. Thermal treatment at 420°C converted samples to KCaPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002), confirming mass loss is associated with recrystallization by partial thermal dehydration of K3CaH(PO4)2 phase. After treatment at 710°C, patterns correspond to KCaPO4 phase in all cases indicating complete conversion. The 31P NMR MAS spectra of precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate (Godinot et al., 2017) (Fig. 4). The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphate compounds, such as hydroxyapatite and octocalcium phosphate (Frossard et al., 1994). The signal at δ = 0.74 ppm is related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with KCaPO4 formation. A shift was also observed at around δ = -5 ppm (marked at δ = -4.78 ppm) in sample milled by 2 h at 600 rpm, attributed to pyrophosphate formed by phosphate dimerization (Godinot et al., 2017). The kinetic study of nutrient release was first evaluated in citric acid solution (2 wt%) according to MAPA (2014) (Fig. 5). Phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples, showing phosphates obtained by milling improve nutrient management maintaining bioavailability. Calcium release is rather different for eggshell versus milled samples, with extremely slow kinetics evidencing solubility of phosphates formed. Nutrients release curves were fitted using linear forms of pseudo-first order, pseudo-second order, and intraparticle diffusion models. Phosphorus and potassium presented better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering R² and values related to concentration at equilibrium time 'qe' and 'experimental qe' (Table 1). For both nutrients, there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing and related to formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases. Even not possible to compare kinetic constants for calcium release, an opposite effect was observed: new phosphate phases from milling made calcium readily available. Thus, considering kinetic behavior, these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying bioavailability of P and K (highly soluble from KH2PO4) and increasing calcium bioavailability. The soil release essays (Fig. 6) indicate temporal profile for precursor KH2PO4 shows P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days, keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor. The introduction establishes reverse logistics as an instrument of economic and social development, enabling the collection and restitution of solid waste for reuse, and highlights eggshells as important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite).
